A series of reports of how sages broke bread on Shabbat, with explanations; practices cited as evidence, no event.
A sage reports that colleagues agreed with him on two rulings and not a third; scholarly discussion, speech only.
A halakhic question put to R. Tanhum and the opening of his homily; speech only, no conflict or event.
R. Anani teaches publicly and R. Ami hears and becomes angry; mainly speech, but with conflict and an emotional reaction.
Rabba bar Rav Huna makes a tambourine, his father comes and breaks it and instructs him otherwise: several actions and a change.
Scholarly exchange between Rav Yehuda and Ulla about a ruling; ordinary dialogue, no event.
A legal case of two claimants with witnesses, framed for legal analysis; no narrated event or change.
Philosophers question the Sages in Rome and receive an answer; a question-and-answer dialogue with no event.
R. Hiyya bar Yosef reports Rav's ruling to Shmuel, who retorts sharply; standard rabbinic discourse, not conflict in R-C2's sense.
Rav Kahana's visit and Rav's instruction are cited as legal evidence; a bare report with nothing following.
Rav Pappa's interrupting his meal is cited as a precedent; a bare report of what he did.
A dialogue between a heretic and R. Hanina about Balaam's age; speech only, without conflict or event.
An incident (a barrel leaks, a gentile jumps and plugs it) followed by Rav Pappa's ruling; real actions, but resolved only by a ruling.
Rav Yosef turns his face away in anger at Rav Huna, and Rav Amram's fringes incident is cited; mainly speech with conflict plus an alluded incident.
Reports of the habitual practices of Shmuel, Rav Huna and Rava with such bread; customs that lead nowhere.
A report that Rabban Gamliel's court nullified a decree, then a scholarly question and answer; no narrative.
An eyewitness report of a rabbi crossing to his student, cited as proof and disputed; a bare report in legal discussion.
A man testifies before R. Hanina and is questioned; a courtroom question and answer with no narrated change.
Famine and plague strike and the Sages deliberate how to pray; real events, but mainly speech and no outcome narrated.
Two incidents only named, each followed by a ruling of liability; nothing beyond the case and ruling is narrated.
The Sages challenge Rava, he reveals his bribes, they look upon him, and King Shapur's men imprison him: actions, causality and change.
An elder explains R. Yohanan's reasoning to R. Ami; teaching only, no event.
A halakhic proof carried between Babylonia and R. Yirmeya and back to Rava; all transmission and retort, the 'foolish Babylonians' jibe is ordinary scholarly sharpness.
Rav's prediction and his students' challenge; teaching and questioning only, no event.
Ravina comes before Rav Ashi and receives a ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event, nothing changes after.
A small real incident (the attendant hands R. Yohanan the wrong sandal, he reacts) cited as evidence; an event and a response but minimal change.
Elisha goes to bring Gehazi to repentance and is refused; an exegetical narrative about biblical figures.
A sick visit that only frames a halakhic question and answer and an explanation afterwards; the setting is not a second event (Shabbat 147a).
Levi's circumstance brought before Rav Sheshet and a ruling; no further narrated action or change.
A bare report that Rav Ashi ruled a certain way in a case involving orphans.
A one-line allusion to R. Tarfon's prohibition cited as evidence, followed by legal discussion; a single ruling with no change.
The Sages resolve to appoint R. Abbahu; seeing R. Abba's debts he defers to him. Real events and motive, but the outcome is only implied.
R. Yohanan denies his own teaching and Rabba bar bar Hana swears by God that he said it; speech only, but with real conflict.
Shmuel demands a source from Rav Mattana and receives an exegesis; question and answer without event.
Two estate cases (a bequest, a division of property) followed by rabbinic discussion of the law; no further action or change.
Rav Pappa decreed a fast in Mehoza, rain fell, he had them recite hallel before eating; real events with change, but told tersely as a precedent in a legal argument.
A report of Shmuel's repeated practice cited as evidence; nothing follows.
The market walk frames only a question and answer, but Shmuel's father finding donkeys and returning them after twelve months is a real incident, alluded to briefly as an exemplum.
R. Eliezer b. R. Yosei's refutation of the Samaritans is speech only, but a polemical confrontation with real conflict.
Rabbi rebuffs R. Natan and later retracts, confessing he was insolent in his youth; mainly speech, with conflict and a change of heart.
An apostate's taunt to R. Hanina, answered by R. Oshaya, and the apostate's concession; a speech confrontation with conflict and no further event.
R. Yosei b. R. Hanina's instruction to his servant to store produce, cited as practice; a single act that leads nowhere.
Rabbi's childhood reading is cited as evidence for a view and rejected in argument; a bare report followed by legal discussion.
A halakhic question and an exchange about whether it is a good question; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
A visit framing a question about Rava's blessing practice and his answer; a setting plus question and answer is not enough.
The emperor challenges Rabban Gamliel, who strikes the emperor's servant to stage a demonstration and wins the argument; action beyond speech, conflict and resolution.
A needle case brought before rabbis who give no ruling; coming before them is the only event and the rest is legal reasoning.
An incident only cited as a precedent (Rabbi granted four nights) within an objection; one ruling with nothing narrated.
Shmuel's instruction to a scribe about deed wording, cited as legal evidence; speech only.
Habitual practices of Abaye's mother and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's attendant cited as evidence; customs that lead nowhere.
Rav arrives in Tatlefush, overhears women, concludes they are ignorant, stays and enacts a prohibition on udders; several actions leading to a change.
A deed signed by robbers comes before Rav Pappa bar Shmuel and Rava rules; a case and ruling with no other narrated action or change.
Exegetical narrative of Joshua and the angel at Jericho; a biblical episode elaborated midrashically.
Judges in two towns collected slaves from orphans and Rav Nahman ordered them returned under threat; events and conflict, but the outcome is only implied by his order.
A question Rava does not understand and Ravina clarifies; ordinary dialogue about a term with no event or conflict.
A one-line eyewitness wonder ('I myself saw') about the height of Keren Ophel; an open case between report and story.
Ben Katin making twelve spigots is a bare report of what someone did, cited as evidence for a legal inference.
Students' question and R. Shimon b. Yohai's parable; the parable is hypothetical and the exchange is teaching.
A custom of city dwellers bequeathing lulavim, cited as proof and rejected; a habitual practice with no event following.
Ravina's twelve-month delay is reported as a precedent for a legal rule; one act with no narrated change.
A damaged-ceiling case followed by two rabbis' rulings; one event then rulings, nothing changes afterwards.
Ravina visits Sura and is asked about his teaching and answers; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
A halakhic dilemma, a disagreement and a question put to Rava, who rules. Speech and scholarly Q&A only; nothing happens.
Incidents only alluded to as precedents (Shmuel and R. Yohanan collecting half, the coronation tax divided by Rabbi). Real events, but too little is narrated.
An encounter that only frames a scholarly back-and-forth. The closing jibe is ordinary Talmudic retort, not conflict in the R-C2 sense.

Firstborn sells the property, the orphans eat dates, the buyers beat them, relatives protest, Rava rules: several actions, conflict and a resolution. Segment 3 is the Gemara's analysis of the ruling and is excluded.
A report of Rav's habitual practice (washing, blessing, teaching) cited as evidence, with nothing following.
Rav appointing a disseminator to teach a contrary ruling is teaching, i.e. speech; no event or change.
Rabbi Yosei's lecture leads to 300 break-ins, the townspeople harass him, he responds, and at his death the gutters run with blood: causally linked events with change.
A dialogue between a heretic and R. Abbahu with real conflict (he accuses him of cursing), but nothing beyond speech.
Rava bar Shmuel visits the Exilarch and breaks bread at once, against his own ruling, and is challenged and explains. An event, but mainly a question and answer with little change.
One event (Rav Huna's crop harvested on the festival), then a legal objection and answer; nothing changes afterwards.
Rav Sheshet meets Rabba bar Shmuel and asks what he teaches; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
A woman tries to take dust from under R. Hanina's feet for sorcery, and he dismisses her with a verse: a real act and conflict, but no outcome or change narrated.
A garden fertilized with idolatrous dung, a query sent and a ruling given; the case brought to a rabbi is the only event.
A historical account of successive ordinances culminating in Yehoshua ben Gamla's reform. It has change and causality but describes general practices, not a narrated incident.
A bird falls into kutah, Rav Hinnana permits it, and Rava praises the ruling: one event, then a ruling and discussion.
Basket sellers come to town, the townspeople block them, and Ravina rules. There is an incident with conflict before the ruling, but no change is narrated, and the remainder is legal commentary.
Shmuel's father sends notched knives to Eretz Yisrael as a halakhic query and receives an answer; effectively a question and answer.
An incident (a fox clawing a ewe brought before the Sages) cited inside the legal give-and-take: one event, then a ruling, with variant versions debated.
The students laugh at Rav bar Shaba and Rav Kahana rebukes them: speech with conflict (mockery) but no event beyond speaking.
Three sages sit and trade teachings; the content is instruction, and Rava's practice when sick is a habitual report that leads nowhere.
A seating and a sighting serve only as the setting for an identification of a fabric; the rest is ordinary scholarly exchange with no conflict or change.
R. Yohanan's visit to Parod and his response to R. Tanhum's teaching is a real event, but it is mainly speech: a question, a teaching and a praising verse.
A son questions his father's change of teaching; this is teaching and scholarly back-and-forth with no narrated event.
Students misunderstand a statement and R. Yirmeya clarifies it. This is pure discussion of meaning.
Ulla sitting on a damaged idolatrous platform is a real act that draws a challenge, but what follows is a halakhic debate made entirely of speech.
This is an aggadic narrative about Gabriel and the founding of Rome, set on Solomon's marriage, an exegetical narrative built on a biblical event.
Shmuel threatens the myrtle sellers, which is a speech act with conflict cited as evidence of his view. Nothing narrated follows from it.
R. Zeira's travels and encounters as he traces a teaching's attribution are real events, but they are mainly about transmitting a teaching, with weak change.
One rabbi accepts an explanation and another rejects it, and they argue over baraitot. This is standard rabbinic dialogue with no events.
A challenge from a baraita and a retraction is ordinary legal back-and-forth.
R. Huna bar Sehora feeding R. Hamnuna, and his remark, is a real incident cited as a proof. It has little change, and the Gemara's analysis that follows in segment 3 is commentary.
The students' claim angers Rava (an emotional reaction) and he rebukes them. This is mainly speech, though there is conflict.
A dying man's statement about his wife is followed only by debate and a ruling to be concerned, with no further narrated action or change.
R. Zeira reports his own practice at his wedding as evidence. It is a bare report that leads nowhere.
A man buys land next to his father's estate and asks for his portion there, and Rabba rules. These are real events, but the ruling ends the passage and nothing changes afterwards.
A question is sent, Rav Huna dies before it reaches him, and his son answers in his name. There are real events, but the passage is mostly halakhic transmission.
An incident is only named as the reason for a decree, and none of it is narrated.
Shmuel recounts the day the king's army came and he prayed alone. The events are real but are cited as evidence for a ruling, with little development.
An unspecified incident is brought before Shmuel and he rules on it. Coming before the rabbi is the only event.
A single incident (a fetus's spasms after the mother died) is alluded to as a legal proof and explained away. It has no narrative development.
An ox injures a child and the case comes before Rava, who rules and answers a challenge; one event then a ruling with nothing changing after, which Jeff ruled is not a story.
A bare report of Mareimar's collection ruling followed by ordinary scholarly challenge and answer.
Rabba testing his students is a question and answer exchange with no event beyond speech.
Ravina permits beer, Rav Hiyya pours wine instead, Ravina is unconcerned: real events but little change, inside a legal discussion.
Exegetical narrative about Jacob and the premature sunset, built on biblical events.
Rabbi Yohanan's distress and the Sages ordaining one scholar but not the other are real events, but cited briefly as evidence with little narrative development.
Rabbi asks Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon a question on the road and they answer; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
Elijah's conversation with Rav Yehuda is mainly dialogue, though events (the Yom Kippur sins in Neharde'a) are mentioned; segment 3 drifts into exposition.
Reports of what Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yannai did, met with skeptical remarks; no incident and no change.
Rabbi Hiyya throws a clod at the moon and addresses it, then Rabbi sends him to sanctify the month; real actions but little causality or change.
Rav sits outside, is brought felt cloths and declines them, onlookers misread his reason; several actions but weak change, framed as evidence for his view.
Rabbi Ile'a searches among the students and Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov concedes; some action and change, but mainly about transmitting a teaching.
A question about what Rav said and how to understand his silence; pure dialogue without conflict.
A setting of two sages sitting on a porch framing the reporting of rulings; no event follows.
A question about a document is sent to Abaye and he rules; a case and ruling with no further narrated action.
Ravina's instruction to his mother serves only to raise a halakhic objection and answer; no event or change is narrated.
Exegetical narratives of Abraham's exchanges with God, built on biblical verses.
At Rav Hisda's funeral the mourners intend practices and Rabbi Yitzhak and Rabbi Yitzhak bar Ami correct them; a real occasion but mainly rulings with implied change.
Reports of when sages ate new grain, cited as evidence of their views; practice with nothing following.
An attendant brings a case of exposed water to Rav Hilkiya, who rules, and the Gemara disagrees; one event then a ruling.
An eyewitness report of what R. Yohanan did, cited as evidence in a legal argument; nothing follows from it.
A visit framing a halakhic challenge and answer; the setting only frames the question (Shabbat 147a shape) and the exchange is ordinary scholarly discourse.
R. Yehuda raises a difficulty before R. Akiva, who retracts his teaching; speech and a quasi-speech act within normal scholarly discourse, no event.
A report of the habitual practice of R. Ami and R. Asi, cited as evidence, leading nowhere.
A polite question and a poetic answer about old age; speech only, without conflict or event.
A halakhic question-and-answer exchange while walking in the market; the setting only frames it.
A report that scribes were asked and knew the law, cited as evidence; no narrative development.
A polemical encounter between the emperor and Rabban Gamliel, mainly dialogue with conflict, with the emperor's groaning as a minor event.
Real events (purchase of the loft, repossession by the creditor) followed by a case before Shmuel and his ruling plus a challenge; weak continuation after the ruling.
R. Asi's silence, R. Zeira later finding him teaching, and the admission that the law came back to him: mainly speech and teaching, with a small narrated change.
Rava's instruction to his attendant is cited within the legal give-and-take as evidence; no narrated event.
A host poses a halakhic question to Rav Adda and receives an answer; question and answer only.
Rav Hisda meets Rabba bar Shmuel and asks what he learned; a scholarly question and answer.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi a halakhic question about collecting a debt and gets a ruling; nothing happens afterward.
Rav Ashi's sadness (an emotion, which counts as an event) at failing to prepare an eruv tavshilin opens a mainly halakhic dialogue.
A report that the tannaim were asked and their versions differed; a scholarly inquiry, not an event.
A legal dictum and Rava's general instruction to his servant about when to light; instruction and question, no event.
Intestines come before Rava, his comparison fails, his son rubs them and they match, Rava questions him and praises him: several actions, a change and a resolution.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi how to prepare knives for Passover; a question and answer with no event.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak puns on his name; speech without conflict or event.
A found object (date pit) and a remembered ruling of Rav Kahana; a case and a ruling with no other narrated action or change.
A halakhic question put to Rav and his answers; question and answer only, no event or conflict.
A dream reported and interpreted; mainly speech, though the interpretation tells of the battalions plotting and dying.
Bar Hamdudei's report of Shmuel standing at a phrase of the confession, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows.
A heretic's challenge to R. Ami answered with a parable; speech with conflict, and the parable's events are hypothetical.
Rav Huna points at Rav Yehuda while illustrating, and Rav Yehuda takes offense: an act and an emotional reaction, minimal development.
An unpaid dinar on a donkey sale prompts a legal discussion among rabbis; the incident leads to a ruling and nothing changes.
King Shapur mocks Shmuel and Shmuel retorts; speech only, but with conflict.
Rabbi asks R. Yehoshua b. Korha the source of his longevity, with a tense exchange; dialogue with some conflict, no event.
Rav Hisda recounts reciting Grace at the Exilarch's and Rav Sheshet's angry reaction, which now leads him to refuse to teach; events with conflict and consequence.
Rav Yehuda falls ill, recovers, and is visited by the Sages who bless God; real events, then a halakhic remark, with little development.
Rav Huna challenges his son Rabba for not attending Rav Hisda and rebukes his answer; dialogue with some conflict and implied change.
A halakhic question and answer between Rav Aha and Rav Ashi.
A single event (an old man crushed in the Temple court) with a consequence (the Passover named for it); a report with little development.
Rami bar Abba asks two rabbis whether he may demolish an old synagogue and both prohibit; a case brought for a ruling, nothing further narrated.
Agrippa's steward asks R. Eliezer two halakhic questions and receives answers; question and answer, the retort is ordinary discourse.
Rav recounts Rabbi changing his ruling overnight, and Rav retracting while absent Levi did not; mainly teaching and quasi-speech acts, with some change.
Rav Hiyya bar Avin loses meat, comes before Rav Huna, and is told he may take it; one event and a ruling.
Thieves come and a bailee hands over a deposited cup, then Rabba exempts him and Abaye objects; real events followed by a ruling and legal discussion.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda reports a case he judged and Rava orders the decision reversed; the incident is only sketched and the rest is legal dialogue, though the reversal implies change.
A prayer leader repeats 'emet' before Rabba and Rabba mocks him: one small event and a mocking retort, mainly speech with some conflict.
An incident only cited as precedent: a case at Rav Kahana's and his prohibition, with no further narrated action or change.
Mainly teaching and objection, but Rava then appoints an interpreter and publicly retracts his ruling, an act with change.
Cases brought before Rabbi Yohanan and his rulings, discussed as legal precedent; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
Reports a scholar's habitual circumventions on Shabbat, raised to Rav Ashi who rules; actions exist but they are practices cited for a halakhic point with little change.
A dictum attributed to the Angel of Death: content of speech with no narrated event or conflict.
Rav Kahana's retrospective remark about his exile and a short exchange; the exile is only mentioned, not narrated.
A case came before Rabbi Ami and he ruled; no further action or change is narrated.
An exchange of taunts between two heretics; pure dialogue but with conflict.
The wives' habitual peeling of barley is cited as evidence for a halakha, a custom that leads nowhere.
A man builds on the orphans' land, ignores Rav Nahman's order to appease them, and Rav Nahman confiscates the mansion: several actions, conflict and a change.
Rav Yosef states what he would do upon hearing a ruling; a hypothetical intention in speech, not an event.
A report of Ravina's father's practice cited for its halakhic view; a custom with nothing following.
A bare report of how Rav dissolved Rabba's vow, cited as evidence for the halakha.
A one-line report that Ravina ruled in a case, cited as precedent.
Rava tests his students with a contradiction and they answer; ordinary scholarly discussion, no event.
An incident alluded to as a challenge in the legal discussion, a single observed fact with no development.

Rava lets the Sages leave after four cups, Rava bar Livai is injured, and Rava attributes it to his challenge in the lecture; real events with a causal claim, but sketched as evidence for Rava's view.
Mustard prepared and refused, with Ze'eira's wife's reproach; small events and a mild conflict, cited as halakhic practice, with little change.
After Rav Sheila's lecture Rav appoints an interpreter and publicly counters him; mainly teaching, but a public act of rebuttal with conflict.
A question put to R. Eliezer and his dismissive answer; speech only, a question and answer with no event beyond speaking.

Mostly a description of recurring miracles under Shimon HaTzaddik (custom-like reports); the one incident, a priest taking his fellow's portion and being nicknamed 'son of a robber', is a minimal event with a consequence.
R. Abba meets Rav's students and they exchange teachings; scholarly dialogue with no event beyond speech.
A dying man writes a get and sighs, his wife promises to remarry him, then Rav Zevid rules; real events and emotion but no narrated change after the ruling.
Ravin and Abaye walk, see willows, disagree, and Ravin peels the bark to show him; several actions and a resolution of the dispute.
A report of R. Hanina's habitual ability at eighty and his explanation of it; no one-time event and nothing follows.
A dead mouse found in Rav Ashi's storeroom and his instruction to remove it, cited as legal proof; one event and a ruling, outcome only implied.
A habitual report that a blind neighbor judged and R. Yohanan said nothing, raised as a legal difficulty; nothing happens or changes.
Exegetical narrative of fiery vessels descending and Moses copying them; biblical figures.
Midrashic elaboration of King Amon's sin and his exchange with his mother; biblical characters.
Two brothers divide an estate, one builds a wall darkening the other's hall, they quarrel, and Rav Hama rules; multiple narrated acts and conflict before the ruling, like the cow case.
Reports of Rav's practice in ordering Shema, tefillin and prayer, cited and debated in the legal give-and-take; no story develops.
Child Abaye and Rava are tested by Rabba; Rava points to the ceiling, Abaye goes outside and points to the sky, and Rabba foretells their greatness; actions beyond speech with a resolution.
A passerby's proverb and Shmuel's matching verse; speech only, no conflict or event.
A report of Rav Aha bar Yaakov's habitual lulav practice and saying, followed by the Gemara's comment; a custom that leads nowhere.
A guarantor repays a gentile creditor and the sages debate the law; one event then legal discussion, nothing else narrated.
R. Tzadok's conduct with less than an egg-bulk is cited from a mishna as legal proof; a bare report of practice.
Rav Nahman's statement that he changed his judicial practice after hearing a teaching; a report of practice in speech, not a narrated incident.
Rav Ashi's one-line report that he dreamt of a goose and then rose to greatness; two events with minimal causality and little development.
A brick falls into R. Hiyya's wife's oven and he gives an oblique instruction, cited for the law; one event and a ruling whose outcome is only implied.
Short reports of rabbis moving a lamp and the host becoming angry: real events with an emotional reaction, but cited as evidence of practice with little development.
One-line eyewitness wonder (Rabba saw the angel Ridya); an open case between report and story, so borderline is preferred.
One real event (a duck arrives with a bloody neck at Rava's house) followed mainly by deliberation and Rava's praise of his son; mainly speech around one event.
Rav Eina teaches publicly and Rabba orders his interpreter removed: speech with real conflict and an implied public consequence, but no narrated event beyond speech.
One event (the vizier's men deposit wine with sharecroppers) followed only by the rabbis' reasoning and Rava's ruling; nothing else changes.
Scholarly exchange, but Rava suspects he is being put off, goes out, checks and discovers the baraita: a small action and change beyond ordinary dialogue.
A sack of dinars arrives and R. Ami rushes to acquire it, then the Gemara discusses its legality; real events but little development, between report and story.
A man comes before R. Ami, is sent to R. Abba bar Memel, who rules; coming before a rabbi and a ruling with no other narrated change.
Incident with distinct actions (thieves come, he hands over the captives' fund), brought before Rabba who rules, with Abaye's challenge: the cow-case shape of incident plus ruling.
An incident only alluded to in debate (a bird hissed on a field and a stone broke its head), two events but sketched as an objection.
Rava's instruction to his attendant is cited only as evidence of his halakhic view; a bare report of speech with nothing following.
The Ben Zakkai fig-stems incident is only alluded to as a source for a dispute, not narrated.
A man dies, people ask Rav Nahman to eulogize him and he refuses with a quip; an event and a response, but mainly speech.
R. Yohanan falls ill, prepares the remedy on Shabbat and is cured, then is questioned by R. Hiyya bar Abba; real events and change but embedded in legal discussion with little development.
Hunters' habitual practice brought before R. Abba for a ruling; no narrated change beyond the ruling.
A single event (a jug burst) cited in passing as evidence in a legal argument, without change or causality.
The Gemara's explanation of a story told elsewhere (Shimon HaTzaddik's vestments); commentary, not the story.
Rav Pappa's question, Rav Yehuda's silence and Rav Pappa's own reasoning are scholarly discussion with no event or conflict.
Rav Avya's hand dislocates, he asks about treatments, and meanwhile it heals; real events and a change, but mainly a halakhic exchange with weak causality.
A letter about Ukvan's complaint against his brother: conflict and an alluded wrong, but conveyed entirely through correspondence.
A practice brought before R. Yehuda ben Beteira and his ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event beyond the ruling.
One real incident (the bull, Rav Yitzhak taking choice meat as a demonstration) followed by R. Zeira's remark; little change or development.
A wonder about Shapur's snake swallowing straw, alluded to as evidence inside a legal discussion; real events but only sketched.
A setting (Abaye finds Rav Yosef in mourning dress) framing a question and answer; ordinary scholarly exchange with no change.
A single act of R. Akiva mentioned in passing to identify an ornament; no continuation.
A report of R. Tzadok's practice cited as evidence; nothing follows from it.
Eyewitness report of R. Yohanan's conduct cited for halakhic inferences; no response or change.
Rav's crop harvested on the festival and Shmuel's dismay (an emotional reaction) form a minimal incident, then legal discussion.
Rav Hilkiya's farming practice leads to a doubled yield and sale as fine flour; events and change but little drama, cited as demonstration.
R. Shimon's one-line 'I saw' inside a legal baraita, followed by discussion; a report, not a narrated incident.
Permission to teach and a public teaching; speech only, no conflict.
Rav Pappa transfers his loans, Rav Shmuel bar Aha collects and returns, Rav Pappa goes out to meet him; several actions and a change, but brief and cited as legal illustration.
Dialogue between R. Eliezer and R. Akiva with real conflict (a curse foretelling his death); speech only, so borderline.
An instruction and Rav Sheshet hearing a sound and remarking on it, followed by the Gemara's analysis; no development or change.
A poor man comes, Rav Pappa refuses him, Rav Sama challenges; conflict with an event, but mainly a legal exchange and no stated outcome.
R. Elazar's eyewitness report of the curtain in Rome cited as evidence; the background is the translator's addition, not the text.
Jugs found and Rava permits them, then legal discussion; one event plus a ruling with nothing changing afterward.
A visit framing a halakhic practice (spreading a cloth and reciting kiddush), cited with a baraita; setting plus practice is not enough.
Rav Yosef's wife lights late, is rebuked, overcorrects, and an elder corrects her; mainly speech but with actions and some change.
Rabbis pass through the market and say nothing; a report cited as evidence of their view.
Rav Pappa challenges Rava with Ravin's letter, and Rava appoints an amora and publicly retracts his teaching. Mainly speech, but the public retraction is a change that follows the challenge.
This describes Rabbi Hiyya's habitual practice when cases came before him. No single event happens and nothing follows from it.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna come before Rava, they talk about their studies and the land they bought, and he proclaims a verse about them. Mainly dialogue, with events reported only inside it.
This only cites the mishna's incident by its opening words as a heading, and none of it is narrated. A named-only incident like this is not a story.
Antoninus and Adrakan served Rabbi and Rav, and when each died the rabbi lamented. There are events (habitual service, a death, a reaction), but there is little development.
A report, cited for its law, that the Sages dissolved a vow and told the man to pray for forgiveness. It is a ruling with no further narrated change.
Rabbi Elazar's dream of Rabbi Yohanan is cited only to support his explanation of the verse. A single act, cited as evidence, that leads nowhere.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Nahman, who questions it and attributes it. This is ordinary scholarly exchange with no event.
Rav Asi's practice of reciting havdala is cited as evidence of his view. A bare report of practice.
A land dispute brought with one witness, followed by the scholars' legal analogy. It is a court case with no other narrated action or change.
A Levite's habitual snatching is reported to Rav, who only comments. Nothing follows from it.
An elder tells Rabbi Yirmeya how Rabbi Yohanan introduced a topic. This is teaching and speech only.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rav Adda bar Ahava corrects it. Ordinary scholarly exchange.
A man contracted to plant sesame planted wheat instead, which yielded more, and the Sages then discuss the split. The incident has two acts and a change, but it is followed only by legal discussion.
Rav Geviha's public teaching, Ameimar's challenge and Rav Ashi's defense make up a standard halakhic dialogue with no event or conflict beyond it.
Rav Pappa reports that Rava tested them with a contradiction between sources. This is teaching and speech only.
Rabbi Yohanan's consoling saying is cited only as evidence of which view is his. The deaths of his sons are context in the gloss, not narrated.
Shmuel meets Rav's students and asks what Rav taught, and they answer and he comments. Meeting them only frames a question and answer.
Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok travel to Lod to intercalate the year, stop for Shabbat in Ono and rule there. There are real events, but they lead only to a ruling, with little change.
Mar Zutra divided the peppers equally with his brothers, came before Rav Ashi and lost his double portion by the ruling. An act and then a ruling, close to the shape of the cow case.

A collective history of bathhouse decrees: attendants and bathers evade, the Sages respond in stages and finally relent. Real events and change, but no individual protagonist and told as a legal etiology.
Josiah sequestering the Ark is a biblical king's act, outside the rabbinic and post-biblical scope.
R. Yishmael's vow resists dissolution, a launderer strikes him, and he then dissolves it himself. Several actions, conflict and a change.
Rabbi reports a word he heard on travels, cited only to explain a verse; nothing happens.
Reports of what Rav and Mar bar Ravina habitually did not allow, cited as practice; no event follows.
Rav sighs while Rav Kahana reads, and Kahana draws an inference. A minimal event and reaction; the rest is exegesis.
Ben Stada's act is only alluded to as evidence in a debate, followed by genealogical discussion; a single act with no development.
An observation about R. Yohanan's body and an explanation; speech with no event or conflict.
R. Yannai sees a man give charity publicly and rebukes him: one real event followed by speech, cited as illustration.
Two cases of a borrowed ax that broke, brought before Rava and Rav, with rulings and a challenge to Rav. Incident plus ruling, with little further change.
R. Zeira and Rav Asi exchange halakhic information; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
Ravina arranges his son's marriage, sets a date, then delays the wedding a week. Narrated actions with a change.
A youth sells property and frees his slaves, and Rava voids the sale; an incident with a ruling, embedded in a discussion of how the ruling was inferred.
A scholar challenges a judge's ruling, threatens to bring a letter, and goes to Rav Hama, who upholds the judge. Conflict and some action, but mainly speech.
R. Akiva reports a word heard in Arabia, cited for a lexical point; no event.
R. Hama eats, his attendant refuses, and he tells him to eat citing a tradition. Small events, mainly a ruling in speech.
A slaughterer sells tereifa, is removed by Rav Nahman, shows remorse, Nahman considers reinstating him, and Rava objects. Multiple actions and change.
Exegetical narrative about Miriam, Amram and Moses' birth; a biblical episode retold.
Rav Huna reports his sisters' practice as evidence for a ruling; no event.
A habitual situation (a blind neighbor judging, R. Yohanan silent) cited as a legal difficulty; nothing happens and nothing follows.
A man cuts down another's palm, is judged by the Exilarch, rejects the ruling and goes to Rav Nahman: several actions, conflict and change. Segment 3 is Rava's legal challenge, not narrative.
R. Hananya Kara's report that R. Hanina permitted dividing verses only for children is speech about a permission, cited as evidence; no narrated event or change.
R. Ila climbs the stairs and hears a child reading a verse, then reacts in speech, followed by Rav's exegesis; one real event, mainly speech.

An incident cited as evidence: buds were removed and the pomegranate withered while the caper survived; events with causality but no protagonist and told only as proof. Segment 3 is the halakhic conclusion.

Abba Elazar's one-time incident of bringing a calf to the women's court so women could lay hands on it is a real event with motive, but is cited as evidence with little change; the rest is legal inference.
A habitual practice (carrying oil and towel for R. Shimon to the spring) cited as proof of discipleship; a custom that leads nowhere.
R. Yirmeya visits Savta, sees the practice and prohibits it: a setting, one event and a ruling with nothing changing afterwards, followed by a parallel dictum.
Two students report their dreams and Rava interprets them; the dreams are experiences but the passage is almost wholly speech without conflict or change.
Rabba bar bar Hana's 'I saw the place and it was three parasangs' is a one-line eyewitness observation used as evidence, inside a biblical exegesis; nothing follows.
Rav Zevid's tenants stole produce and he disqualified them as witnesses: a real misdeed and a consequential act, but terse and essentially one event plus a ruling.
A bare report that Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava declared items ownerless, cited as a challenge; no continuation.
A man struck another and came before R. Yehuda Nesia, who ruled he pay a Tyrian maneh: one event, then a ruling cited as proof, with nothing further narrated.
Ben Azzai follows R. Akiva into the privy, observes and learns, and is rebuked by R. Yehuda and answers: actions, an unusual confrontation and a reply.
A priest poured the libation on his feet and the people pelted him with etrogim: two actions, conflict and a consequence, quoted by the Gemara as a proof (R-C1 keeps the Talmudic citation).
A deathbed instruction followed by Rav Nahman visiting Rav Hisda and a question-and-answer on the law; a setting plus question and answer is not a story (Shabbat 147a).
A barrel of wine was found and Ravina permitted it: one event and a ruling, then legal analysis.
A fire in Drokart spares Rav Huna's neighbourhood, people attribute it to him, and a dream reveals it was a generous woman's merit: events, causality and a reversal.
Rav Yosef weeps over a teaching and Abaye consoles him with a verse; an emotional reaction counts as an event but the passage is mainly speech.
A one-line report that the High Priest's voice was heard in Jericho, with a distance note, in a list of Temple wonders; nothing follows.
A man utters an excommunication formula and asks Rav Hisda, who rules; speech plus a ruling with no other narrated action or change.
Abaye sees Rava gazing west and they exchange a question and answer about a baraita; the setting only frames a halakhic exchange with no further event or change.
The Sages enter the vineyard at Yavne and make a teaching statement with a proof text; speech without conflict or event beyond the setting.
R. Ami finds a vessel of dinars, hesitates, and a Roman tells him to take it; a real event with a response, but mainly speech and the outcome is only implied.
Rabba's habitual practice of opening with a joke before teaching is cited as illustration; a custom that leads to no one-time event or change.
Abaye finds Rabba sliding his son on a donkey and challenges him; the rest is a halakhic justification, ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no further event.
Mar son of Ravina, thirsty in a valley, has a miracle spring created for him and drinks; a narrated event sequence with need, miracle and resolution.
Levi reads from a Megilla before Rav Yehuda, who states the ruling; one event followed by a ruling with nothing changing afterwards.
Rava compelling Rav Natan bar Ami to give 400 zuz is an incident alluded to as precedent; there is an action and outcome but it is barely narrated.
The Sages prayed for mercy and the sound of the departing soul was eliminated; an event with a change, but only a one-line legendary report inside a list of sounds.
A man sells land with a guarantee, negotiates terms, the land is seized and a flood destroys the seller's best land; an actual incident with multiple events and change, preceding a ruling.
A tannaitic exegetical dispute; no narrated event.
Students ask R. Yitzhak ben Elyashiv to pray and he answers that he gave up the power; a request and answer with no event or conflict.
Levi sees a man bang his head in the bathhouse and makes a remark, cited as evidence in a legal discussion; a single observed act with no continuation or change.
A polemical exchange between a Boethusian and R. Yehoshua HaGarsi ending in the Boethusian's concession; speech only, but with conflict and implied change.
R. Asi missed the study hall and asks R. Zeira what was said; the setting frames a halakhic question-and-answer, which is not a story.
Foreign litigants come before Rava who uses an interpreter, then discussion; and a witnesses case resolved by debate. One event followed by legal discussion, no change.
R. Yehoshua married a priest's daughter, fell ill, and interpreted his illness as Aaron's displeasure; two events with an implied causal change and a reaction.
Rav Pappa reports that questions were put to him and how he ruled; teaching and ruling are speech, no event.
Rav's practice of buying wheat via donkey drivers at a set rate is cited as precedent in a legal discussion; a report of what he did with no continuation.
A prayer leader recites the Avoda and Rava corrects his wording; a setting plus a halakhic correction, ordinary scholarly speech.
The Rav Safra sale incident is only alluded to by name ('such as Rav Safra'); the narrative must be supplied by the commentary.
An anatomical observation about a girl in the neighborhood cited as evidence for a physiological claim; no narrated action, response or change.
Reish Lakish eulogizing a scholar is a real event but is mainly his spoken lament, cited as a precedent; little development.
Rav Kahana accompanies Rav Shimi bar Ashi (a real event), but the passage then turns to a scholarly question; mainly speech, no conflict or change.
A case (man sold property, divorced) sent to Rav Pappa for a ruling; the only event besides the case is the legal question and answer.
Two short incidents (Rava seeing Rav Hamnuna pray long; R. Zeira rebuking R. Yirmeya for hurrying) with some action but mainly verbal critique.
Rabbi proposes marriage to R. Elazar b. R. Shimon's widow and she rebuffs him in an exchange of messages; a conflict-laden episode within a larger narrative.
R. Zeira hears a ruling and approves it, followed by Gemara analysis; ordinary transmission of law with no conflict or change.
Rabbi and R. Hiyya walking, R. Yehuda ben Kanosa striding ahead, Rabbi's suspicion, R. Hiyya's defense, and the confrontation: multiple events, conflict and resolution.
Rav Huna's contrary ruling angers Rav Yehuda (emotional reaction) and Rav Huna considers retracting while Rav Hisda counsels him; conflict but mostly legal speech.
Shmuel's instruction to deface Rav Yehuda's seal is cited inside the legal give-and-take as a difficulty; a single alluded act with no development.
An incident where Rav Yosef ruled thirteen animals tereifot, followed only by analysis of his ruling; one event then a ruling.
R. Yohanan's silence is followed by a hypothetical discussion of what he might have answered; scholarly back-and-forth, not an event.
Rava's ruling to the residents of Mehoza with its rationale; a legal instruction, no narrated incident.
R. Yehuda Nesia's actions and R. Ami's dismay are real events with an emotional reaction, but the passage then becomes legal analysis with no further change.
Tanhum arrives and teaches, is challenged for ruling near his teacher, and excuses himself; some event and conflict but mainly speech.
A disputed deathbed gift deed and Rabba's ruling with Abaye's objection; a case and a legal discussion, nothing further happens.
The incident cited is King Hezekiah intercalating the year, a biblical episode.
Binyamin the shepherd's blessing followed by Rav's ruling and Gemara discussion; one act then a ruling.
Rabba bar Rav Huna visiting the Exilarch's house and permitting a practice is a bare ruling report with no further action or change.
Rav Hisda and Avimei exchange a question and an explanation of the mishna; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
A single instruction by Rabbi Zeira to his servant, cited to infer his legal view; speech only, nothing follows.
Disciples ask and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua lists his lifelong practices; a question and answer about habits, with no event.
Reports of Rav's habitual announcement and Rav Amram's habitual practice; no one-time event, nothing follows.
Yohanan the High Priest sent emissaries and saw that only teruma was separated, leading to his decree; real events with a change, but only alluded to as a legal explanation.
A visit that only frames an observation and a remark by Rav Hisda, raised as a legal challenge and resolved; like the Ulla visit, not enough for a story.
Exegetical narrative about David and Hushai built on a biblical episode; biblical characters, out of scope.
A question to Rabbi and his answer pointing to ben Elasa's haircut habit; question and answer plus a practice, no event.
A report that Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Asi ate from a Samaritan's slaughter, cited as evidence, followed by Rabbi Zeira's wondering; no development.
The Sages challenge Rav Sheshet, who becomes angry and retorts; mainly speech, but with conflict and an emotional reaction.
A habitual scene: children sent to Hanan HaNehba grab his cloak and he prays; vivid actions and a prayer, but customary and no stated outcome.
Rav Adda challenges Rav Huna, curses his wife, and Rav Huna's children do not survive while Rav Adda lives; conflict leading to a narrated consequence.
A duck in Mar Shmuel's house whose gizzard was set in the sun and then peeled; real events with a change, but minimal and cited only as a legal proof.
A certain man habitually said a phrase and the Sages drew an inference about his lineage; habitual speech and commentary, no event.
A legal exchange between students before a dozing teacher who wakes and explains; mainly dialogue, with one small event (waking).
Habitual practices of three sages with their ritual fringes; customs that lead nowhere.
Ze'eiri travels to Neharde'a and sends a retraction of a teaching; quasi-speech acts with no conflict or further development.
Eyewitness account: a bird is brought to Rav Ashi, he examines it, finds fifteen sinews and splits one into two; events with a discovery, but minimal and cited as halakhic evidence.
Mar son of Ravina's mother habitually brought him guarded wheat; a practice reported, nothing follows.
Asked a question, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba is silent, then next day publicly teaches; mainly speech and teaching, with a minimal event and implied change.
A sharecropper received land for sesame, planted wheat, and it yielded like sesame; two narrated acts and an outcome, then rulings, the R-C0 cow-case shape.
Rabba bar Yirmeya arriving with a baraita only frames the teaching; the passage is a transmitted law, not an event.
Rava slaps Rav Shimi's sandal and rebukes him: a small physical gesture within ordinary halakhic objection; mainly speech, at most borderline.
Gabriel showing Moses the Candelabrum is an exegetical narrative about biblical figures.
An exchange between a heretic and Geviha ben Pesisa with insults and a threat: speech only, but with real conflict.
Rav Shimi raises a contradiction and Rav answers; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event.
Rav Hisda sees palms among vines and orders them uprooted; one observation and an order whose execution is only implied.
Elijah tells Rav Yehuda the world's span and answers questions; a dialogue conveying teaching, with no conflict or event.
A habitual practice of Rav Hiyya son of Rav Avya cited as evidence; it leads nowhere.
Once Rav Beruna joined redemption to prayer and laughed all day: one event with an emotional consequence, cited as evidence; minimal change.
Rav Pappa tried remedies without success, an Arab advised him, he did it and was healed: several actions and a change.
Abaye's strap tears, he asks and Rav Yosef answers; a setting plus question and answer, as in Shabbat 147a.
A document with an unclear date and a ruling on it; no narrated action beyond the case itself.
Shmuel rending his garment over a sage is a single act cited as evidence of a teacher's status, with no continuation.
Rabba bar bar Hana's 'I have seen' wonder (the reima cub dams the Jordan) is a one-line eyewitness account cited in argument; the open edge of R-C5.
Students are sent to Rav Hananel and return to Rav Huna to resolve a halakhic dilemma; the movement only frames legal transmission and discussion.
A eulogizer's opening words at Rabbi Zeira's death; a quoted speech with no further action or change.
Rabban Gamliel's death leading to Torah study while sitting is an event with a change, but it is a historical report with little narrative.
A gift instruction and a discovered discrepancy brought to Mar Zutra's ruling: one case then a ruling, not a story per Jeff 2026-10-25.
Rabbi Elazar's dream of Rabbi Yohanan only validates his exegesis, followed by an objection and reply; legal discussion.
Exegetical narrative of the prophet Ezekiel and ten men, built on biblical verses; biblical figures, not sages.
A document came before Rabbi, he called it postdated and Zunin corrected him; one real event, then mainly speech, with implied change in Rabbi's knowledge.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports R. Yohanan's habitual practice of washing and donning tefillin before answering; a custom cited as evidence, leading nowhere.
A legal precedent only alluded to (Rav Pappa and Rav Huna's exchange rate for Agardamis's coins); no narrated change.
A single incident (300 priests enlisted to move the vine) cited as evidence of size, with no continuation or change.
Exegetical elaboration on King Jehoiakim's insolence; biblical figure, and mainly speech.
Rav Ashi reports Rav Pappi's habitual practice of reciting kiddush, cited as proof; a custom with nothing following.
Those present laughed at R. Zeira and Abaye rebuked them; speech with conflict (mockery), no event beyond speaking.
Rabban Gamliel weeping at the verse is an emotional reaction, but habitual and mainly speech; sits between borderline and not.
Scholarly question sent from R. Zeira to R. Avin and the ensuing legal give-and-take; quasi-speech acts without conflict.
The Tarbu family goats damaged Rav Yosef's property and Abaye declined to deliver his message; one real event then mainly speech, no change.
An oven smeared with grease and Rava bar Ahilai's ruling; one event followed by a ruling, nothing else changes.

A woman repeatedly brings witnesses who are exposed, then a later incident in which Reish Lakish glares angrily at R. Elazar on discovering the source; multiple actions, conflict and emotional reaction.
A setting (wedding preparations) framing teaching and a question and answer; the setting alone is not enough for a story.
Eyewitness reports of Rava's and Rav Pappi's practice with tefillin blessings; habitual conduct cited as evidence.
Nicanor the Greek general threatens Jerusalem daily, the Hasmoneans defeat him and hang his thumbs and toes; post-biblical figures, multiple actions and change.
Exegetical retelling of Elisha and the bears; a biblical episode elaborated by midrash.
Rabbi's household paid successive bribes until the obligation to bring the fattened ox was abolished; a sequence of actions leading to change.
Rav Pappa slips on a ladder and nearly falls, then a dialogue on its cause; one real event followed by speech with little change.
Rav Nahman's ruling in an actual case is only alluded to within legal discussion; no narrated incident.
A report of what R. Akiva did in prison, cited as evidence and rebutted; nothing follows from the act.
A remark, a suit brought before Rav Nahman and his ruling; coming before the rabbi and being ruled on is the only event, nothing changes.
A man reciting an aphorism and Shmuel citing a verse; speech only, no event or conflict.
A real incident with cause and change (confining the animal in the sun, its death), followed only by a disputed ruling; like the stolen-cow case but minimal.
An incident: a renter took the mezuza and was punished with the death of his wife and two sons, two events with causality and change. Segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary.
Rav Huna sold a cow and explained why when asked; a single act and a question and answer, nothing follows.
Reports of the practice of R. Yohanan and R. Yannai with colleagues disagreeing, then legal discussion; no narrated event leads anywhere.
Ravina wrote an enhanced dowry and negotiated with the groom's family; one real act followed by mainly speech with some tension.
Competing claims between guarantor and debtor and a question sent to Abaye; a legal case of speech and ruling with no narrated change.
Shmuel asked seafarers and reports their answer about a substance; a speech act supplying information, no event or conflict.
A student's question and R. Eliezer's answer followed by Gemara analysis; a question and answer is not a story.
Rav Yehuda corrects his father's teaching and Shmuel rebukes him for how he spoke to his father; all speech, but with interpersonal conflict beyond ordinary debate.
A habitual practice of sages treating drunkenness with oil and salt, cited for the halakha; a custom that leads to no one-time event or change.
A halakhic dispute, a question put to R. Bisa and a verse applied in praise; scholarly speech without an event or real conflict.
R. Hanina's eyewitness report of Rabbi hanging his tefillin, cited as evidence and then discussed; a bare report of an act.
A man's instruction, a question sent to Rav Ashi and his ruling in two versions; no narrated action or change besides the ruling.
R. Tarfon's habitual practice and the Sages' approving remark; a custom that leads to no event.
Brief reports that Shmuel and Rava were served pressed fish and ate it, cited as precedent in a halakhic argument; nothing follows.
Ravina finds Rav Aha searching for a certain herb and challenges him; one real event followed mainly by halakhic speech.
A captive child's offhand account comes before Rabbi, who marries the mother to a priest on its basis; captivity, testimony and an act that changes her status.
Ulla visits and is served white sage, then identifies it as hyssop. The visit only frames a statement, and nothing changes afterwards (cf. Shabbat 147a).
A report of what Yosei ben Yo'ezer did, cited as support, then people come before R. Yannai and he gives a ruling. There is no further narrated action or change.
The people of Nineveh send a halakhic question and Rabbi sends back an answer. That is a question and answer, with no event beyond the speech.
A citation of a Mishnah testimony about a cow eaten as a peace offering. It is a bare report used as legal evidence.

The Rabbis accuse Rava of taking interest over his practice with sharecroppers, and he defends himself. It is all speech, but it carries a real personal conflict, which is more than ordinary scholarly debate.
Rav Hamnuna loses his oxen and Rabba meets him, but that only sets up a scholarly contradiction and its resolution. A setting plus a question and answer is not a story.
Rava answers a halakhic question, and Rav Kahana reports asking the Sages' wives about their practice. These are speech acts and a report of practice, with no event.

Rav Hisda's wife adorns herself, and a student's ruling implicitly criticises her. Rav Hisda answers with an emphatic oath. It is mainly speech, but it carries personal conflict and has a real-life setting.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rav Yitzhak corrects its wording. This is ordinary scholarly exchange, with no event.
Two parties exchange claims over a house and Rava rules. It is a courtroom exchange of speech and a ruling, with no narrated change.

A case comes before Rabba and he rules. Rav Pappa challenges him and he falls silent, and then Gemara discussion follows. This is a case before a rabbi plus normal scholarly challenge, with no real change.
A sale dispute comes before Rav Nahman, who rules, and Rava questions the ruling. There is one event, then a ruling and discussion.
The deception with the reed in Rava's court is only alluded to by name. The translator fills it in from the commentaries.
R. Akiva reports the words he heard on his travels, and the passage uses them for lexical evidence. Nothing happens.
R. Eliezer finds no quorum, frees his slave and completes the ten. That is a minimal incident with a cause and a change, but it is cited inside a legal objection and has little development.

A sharecropper makes a stipulation and leaves a third of the field fallow, and then the Nehardeans and Rava rule. The incident has an action beyond coming to court (like the cow case), but it is thin and is followed only by rulings.
An incident in Pumbedita is only named, and the passage is a scholarly debate about whether an objection holds.
Ben Azzai's dictum about the Sages, with Gemara analysis. It is speech and legal discussion, with no event.
The Sages overhear three cattle herders reciting weather signs and intercalate the year. It is mainly speech, but a real action follows.

R. Elazar realises a Torah scroll is on his bed, slips off in alarm 'like one bitten by a snake', and sits on the ground. It is a single brief incident with an emotional reaction, cited inside a legal argument.
Rav Yosef turns his face in disdain at Rav Huna's ruling, a gesture beyond speech with some conflict, but the rest is halakhic dialogue.
An actual Neharde'a incident (goats ate barley, owner seized them, Shmuel's father ruled) is cited briefly inside the legal give-and-take; real events but only sketched as a precedent.
Rav Huna ate thirteen loaves without Grace, and Rav Nahman responds with a ruling; one real event followed by a rebuke and ruling.
Rabbi Zeira wishes to ascend, does so, and finds Rabbi Elazar to ask about the ruling; there is a journey and a fulfilled wish, but the substance is a halakhic question and answer.
Rabbi Elazar's instruction to his attendant is cited as evidence of his practice; nothing follows.
A habitual avoidance of the wall, then one day Rav Adda bar Ahava comes and Rav declines to detour; mainly speech, with the outcome only implied.
Rav's finding of a hidden scroll is cited only as the source of a teaching, followed by legal discussion.
The grandson comes to Rabbi Yannai, who opens the vow and dissolves it; the dissolution is an act that changes something, though the exchange is mainly speech.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rabbi Elazar clarifies it; ordinary scholarly dialogue without event or conflict.
Rav Yehuda's statement to Ravin about neighboring trees is speech only, with no event or conflict.
Shmuel sends an objection to Rav's ruling; ordinary halakhic disagreement in speech.
Rav Nahman arrives on Yom Kippur eve and ravens drop livers and kidneys; Rav Kahana rules they may be eaten. Real events followed by a ruling, with little development.
A report that Rabbi Ami mourned seven and thirty days, followed by commentary that he acted on his own; the act leads nowhere.
A heretic mocks Berurya with a verse and she retorts; speech with conflict but no event.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef buys a utensil and is told the ruling; one event then a ruling with nothing changing after (Jeff 2026-10-25).
A man asks Rabbi Hiyya for help, Rav goes, inspects, discovers wine in a crack and reverses his ruling; multiple actions and a change.
Rava's distress (an emotional event) and the consolation he receives; little action or change beyond speech.
Rav Beivai's intentions are corrected twice by teachings; intentions and teaching are speech, with no event or conflict.
Rabbis rebuke Rabbi Akiva's exegesis inside a baraita; standard rabbinic exegetical dispute, not a story.
Legal objections and a report of Ameimar's ruling; no narrated event.
R. Yirmeya sees R. Hiyya bar Abba extending his pronunciation and corrects him; one observed act and a remark, mainly speech with little change.
R. Yitzhak Nappaha teaches publicly and Rav Sheshet hears and becomes angry; an emotional reaction and conflict, but almost all speech.
Exegetical narrative about Adam weeping before God and being consoled; biblical characters, not sages.
Homiletic exposition of Moses's rebuke of Israel built on verses; speech and exegesis about biblical figures, no narrated event.
A partnership arrangement brought before Rava who permitted it; one case and a ruling with nothing changing afterwards.
Rav Dimi finds Rav Yirmeya teaching and says he would send a letter if he could; setting plus teaching and a hypothetical, followed by legal discussion.
A heretic challenges R. Abbahu about the order of Psalms and is answered; speech only, but an adversarial exchange with conflict.
Exegetical narrative of Balaam being blinded for his remark; biblical figure.
In Rabbi's era a teaching led everyone to abandon Mishnah, and he then taught the reverse; events with causality and change, but sketched as a summary of teaching.
A document whose witness died and the testimony offered, followed only by Ravina and Rav Ashi's legal discussion; incident then discussion with no change.
R. Zeira cites his own harm (bringing myrtle to the king) against a teaching; an incident only alluded to inside a dialogue.
Rav Oshaya and R. Ami exchange reports of halakhic transmission with strong but ordinary scholarly retorts; speech and legal discussion, no event beyond meeting.
Levi demonstrated a kidda before Rabbi and was lamed; two events and a change, minimal, followed by the Gemara's discussion of the cause.
Rav Mari asks Rava about moving cushions and receives a ruling after a short exchange; a question before a rabbi and a ruling, nothing narrated changes.
A lender demands repayment, the borrower denies the loan, the lender brings witnesses, and Abaye and Rava rule; several actions with conflict, but then only legal rulings.
Rav Safra recounts visiting R. Abba, eating his chicken and being saved from vomiting by old wine; real events with a small consequence, cited as an illustration.
The Exilarch built a house and asked Rav Nahman to affix mezuzot, who instructs him; one event then an instruction, no narrated change.
A bare report that R. Abbahu instituted an order of shofar blasts, followed by legal analysis.
A case of an animal's anatomy, Rav Ashi's inclination and a colleague's correction; case and ruling only.
A man opened windows and came before two rabbis who ruled differently; an incident followed by rulings, with no narrated outcome.
One act (dragging a bench) followed by a rabbi's challenge and legal discussion; ordinary scholarly rebuke with nothing following.
Report of Helene's donation and a habitual phenomenon cited for a halakhic point; no incident or change.
A frame of questions put to R. Yehoshua and his answers, followed by legal discussion; question-and-answer with no event is not a story.
Rav Nahman decrees a fast, rain fails, he despairs and is upset, and rain comes: several events with causal change.
A teaching followed by women going out wearing the ornament: events with some causality but thin, cited as evidence.
Mainly speech about rulings, but Rabbi Tavla acted on a ruling and Rav Nahman threatens him: conflict with some event.
A sage's added comment that Nehunya's son died, with a derashah; commentary on a story told elsewhere, a single reported event.
Shammai's habitual refusal leads to a decree forcing him to feed with two hands: some change, thinly narrated, then discussion.
Habit, then one day Mar Ukva fails to notice Shmuel accompanying him, Shmuel's remark, and Mar Ukva imposes admonition on himself: actions and change.
Rav's report of finding a scroll serves only to cite a teaching and his comment on it; nothing follows.
Rav Hisda's daughter immersed early, caught cold, and died, her bier carried after Rava: multiple events with causality and change.
A polemical exchange between a magus and Ameimar: speech only but with conflict.
Ulla's report that Elul was intercalated and a discussion of its reason; speech and a bare report.
A teaching and the gesture of Rabbis Ami and Asi turning their faces away: mainly speech with conflict and a small act.
Exegetical narrative about the biblical spies and Canaanites.
A claim, a counterclaim and rabbinic rulings; a legal case with no narrated change.
A woman finds blood and comes before R. Yannai, who rules; coming before a rabbi and a ruling is the only event.
Women complain to Rabbi and Rav and receive rulings; nothing further happens.
Mostly legal debate over a document's date, but Rav Aha suspects deflection, goes out, checks and finds Rav Nahman right: a small event and change.
A habitual wonder (goats sneezing from the incense) cited as evidence; no incident develops.

Rav Sheshet's instruction to his attendant to run him past the ashera is a real incident, but it is mainly speech and is immediately absorbed into legal analysis; one event then discussion, leaning borderline.
Two first-person eyewitness sea tales (R. Yohanan and Rav Safra) narrate a voyage and a sighting of wondrous fish, the kind of eyewitness wonder accepted as a story.
A report of Ameimar's practice (having a gentile paint his eye) followed by ordinary halakhic questioning; nothing follows from the act.
Ulla bar Rav leads ne'ila and Rava praises him: a real event with a response, but cited as liturgical evidence with little change; borderline rather than not.
Rabba bar Hana erred in a judgment and came before R. Hiyya, who ruled he must pay; an incident plus ruling used as legal proof, with little narrated change beyond the ruling.
A heretic mocks R. Abbahu and a student arrives with a question; it is mainly speech, but with conflict and a minimal event (the student's arrival).
A baraita recording a halakhic debate between R. Eliezer and R. Yehoshua ending in silence: ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, speech only.
A reported statement ('come and I will show you') cited for an inference; no event is narrated.
A habitual feat of the son of Marta bat Baitos, with his fellow priests not allowing him; events but weak causality and little change.
A bare report of Rav Adda bar Ahava's practice of salting bone by bone; a custom that leads nowhere.
Rava's permission to two scholars is a single ruling cited as precedent, with no other narrated action or change.
An exchange between Yohana and Mamre and Moses, a biblical episode elaborated; at most a speech exchange and about biblical figures.
A document concerning Rav Ilish's sons surfaces and the rest is legal reasoning and debate; one event followed by discussion, nothing changes.
Abaye's boast followed by a scholar's question and his answer is a question-and-answer framed by a setting, then pure legal discussion.
The princes freed by Hezekiah go to Alexandria and build an altar: a narrative about the biblical era, built on Isaiah's prophecy.
Rav Asi's face lights up and R. Yohanan deflates his joy; an emotional reaction inside a halakhic dialogue, mainly speech.
A full narrative of Esau blocking Jacob's burial and Hushim killing him, but about biblical characters, an exegetical narrative.
A dog eats the Sages' shoes, they excommunicate the unknown culprit, and the dog's tail catches fire: multiple actions with causality and change.
A man comes before Rav Huna, a question and answer, and the vow is dissolved; coming before a rabbi and a ruling, with no other action or change.
Jonathan the grandson of Moses as idol priest and his later appointment by David is an exegetical narrative on biblical events.
Elijah's advice to Rav Yehuda followed by halakhic explanation; speech only, no event or conflict.
Rabbi Zeira's eyewitness reports of Rabbi Abbahu's conduct are cited as evidence for halakha, with nothing following.
A note is presented at Rav Huna's court and he rules; Rav Hisda then sends Rabba to investigate. One event plus a ruling and an instruction, a little more than a bare ruling.
Part of the frame story of the visit to Rabbi Yehoshua: mostly the content of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's teaching, ending with Rabbi Yehoshua's response. Teaching is speech.
Abaye reports that Rabba changed his practices after hearing a baraita and Shmuel's statement. There is a change, but these are reports of practice with weak narrative.
A halakhic question to Rav and his reply that he never asked his uncle; ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
A sharp exchange between Rav and Shmuel ends with Rav embarrassed. That is conflict plus an emotional reaction, but it is mainly speech.
Rabbi Hanina ben Akiva went somewhere, found branches and told his students to designate them. This is a small incident cited as a precedent, with little change.
Romans challenge Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya and he answers. It is a polemical exchange with conflict, but speech only.
An anonymous man's aphorism about love, matched to verses; no narrated event.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei recounts refuting the Samaritans. It is a polemical speech with conflict but no event beyond speaking.
Josiah sees the verse and hides the Ark. The actor is biblical, an exegetical narrative about biblical events.
Rabba's halakhic instruction to the binders of the Exilarch's lulav; speech only, no event.

Rav Yosef and Rabba: a query is sent to Eretz Yisrael and answered, Rav Yosef declines the post, Rabba reigns 22 years and then Rav Yosef does, with Rav Yosef's humility throughout. Several actions and a change.
Rava visits the Exilarch, is served breaded goose and eats only after checking it. It is a small incident cited as a precedent and then discussed legally.
Rav Huna dies suddenly, the Sages worry, and Zuga of Hadayeiv reassures them with a teaching. There are real events, but the resolution is speech.
A report that three sages measured the Jordan stones, cited as evidence for a calculation; nothing follows.
Rabbi Yehoshua sends word that Rabbi Yishmael erred, followed by halakhic positions. This is ordinary scholarly disagreement, not conflict in the R-C2 sense.
Rav Mesharshiya's habitual practice of paying a gentile child to sow hops, followed by legal discussion; a custom that leads nowhere.
An exegetical dialogue between Abraham and God expounding a verse; speech only, and biblical in any case.
A short question-and-answer between R. Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav cited to explain his status; speech without conflict or event.
A man is attacked by a lion and miraculously rescued, then comes before Rava who instructs him: an incident with real events and change, followed by a ruling.
An apostate poses a question to R. Abbahu and he answers with a baraita; a question and answer with no narrated event.
Moses ascending on high and his exchange with God is an exegetical narrative about a biblical figure, outside the catalogue's scope.
Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana building his sukka and they exchange views on Rava's ruling; ordinary halakhic dialogue with no change.
Rav Nahman's jug is a bare report, and the Usha incident is only a question put to Rav Asi and his ruling; Rav Yosef's remarks are commentary.
A transmitted teaching about the expansion of the altar; no narrated incident.
Rav Tovi asks Rav Yosef about bringing teruma wine and receives a ruling; a case brought to a rabbi with no further action or change.
A practice of taking dirt from Rav's grave is reported to Shmuel, who rules it permitted; a custom plus a ruling, with nothing following.
Two bare reports of rabbis permitting students to sleep outside or under a canopy, cited as precedents.
Two students pull R. Yitzhak Nappaha in opposite directions and block each other, and he answers with a parable; mainly speech, but with conflict and some action.

R. Yishmael reports that his father's family habitually grazed in forests and judged alone, and that they were destroyed for it; a habit leading to a change, told as a brief report with weak narration.
Shmuel instructs Rav Hana to gather ten men so he can state a halakha publicly; speech only, followed by a ruling.
R. Yirmeya's far-fetched question leads to his removal from the study hall; mainly a question, but one real event and a change follow.

R. Zeira's report culminates with Rabbi retracting his own ruling after hearing R. Hiyya's; mainly teaching and speech, with some travel and a change of position. Segments 3-4 are the Gemara's legal discussion.
Rav Huna sees a man drinking water before havdala and warns him; one event and a remark, with no further action or change.
Mar bar Rav Ashi reports what his father did with a pledged goblet as evidence for a halakhic question; a bare report with no continuation.
Rabbi, moved by what he heard, takes thirteen years of afflictions on himself; a decision with real consequences, part of the larger narrative of Rabbi's sufferings.
Reish Lakish and R. Elazar debate the status of offerings, ending in a sharp retort; standard rabbinic dialogue, not narrative conflict or change.
A folk saying matched by Shmuel to a verse; no event is narrated.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yehuda leaves Rami bar Hama, and when they meet there is a rebuke and a test. Almost everything after the departure is scholarly dialogue.

The Hasmonean candelabrum moves from iron to silver to gold as they grew richer, so there are events and change. It is a historical report cited as proof in a dispute, with weak narrative development.
A man comes before Rava with a threat he received and Rava rules. The only event is coming before the rabbi; nothing else is narrated.
Ulla visits and sees Rabba bar Rav Huna measuring, then there is a question and answer. Like Shabbat 147a, a setting plus a Q&A is not a story.
A habitual practice of Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna is cited as evidence for a ruling. Nothing follows from it.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak disparages Saul, has nightmares, apologizes, has them again and apologizes more fully. A post-biblical sage is the protagonist, with clear causality and change.
The orchard incident (mortgage, three years' use, a threat to hide the deed) is cited as a case type to fix the law. It is sketched, with no outcome narrated.
Antoninus and Rabbi only exchange words; the narrative is the parable of the lame and blind guards, embedded in Rabbi's reply. Mainly speech, with an illustrative fictional story inside.
A bare report that Rav Mari acted on a ruling, with no continuation.
A buyer deliberately overpays so he can sue, the case comes before Rava, and Rava rules. This is an incident with actions beyond the coming-to-court, followed by a ruling, like the cow case.
Rabbi Yohanan asks the money changer for a coin and stops him from rising, then gives a teaching. There are small events, but the passage is mainly a teaching with little change.
R. Zeira's habit of sitting at the study-hall door leads to an encounter with R. Natan bar Tovi. After that the passage is a dialogue about a ruling.
One event (a man sends silk home) followed by R. Ami's ruling and discussion. Nothing else changes.
Rabbi rules, R. Yishmael cites his father, and Rabbi retracts. All of it is speech without conflict.
R. Abba proposes an interpretation and the Sages laugh at him. This is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event.
A one-line report that Rav Huna cut off a hand, cited for his view, with no continuation.
Shmuel HaKatan decrees a fast, rain falls after sunset, the people misread it, and he corrects them with a parable. There are events and a response.
Rav Pappa slips in his speech and fasts in atonement. There are two minimal events with causality, but very little development.
A one-line Gemara explanation about an incident told elsewhere. No incident is narrated here.
A list of bare reports of what sages did to show anger, cited as examples. None leads anywhere.
A bare report that Rav Nahman permitted Yalta to be carried, cited as a precedent and explained away; nothing follows.
Rabbi Zeira arrives and challenges Rabbi Ami, who is astonished and revises his teaching; mainly speech, with some conflict and change.
Mar Zutra Hasida's habitual practice cited to illustrate the law; a custom that leads nowhere.

The sons of Rabbi Hiyya go out to the villages, forget their learning and are distressed, prompting their dialogue; narrated events with an emotional reaction and change, the opening of a known story.
A halakhic question sent and answered, then sent again; quasi-speech acts of transmission with no real conflict or event.
Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish exchange views and a quip; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, no event.
Rav Kahana reports a personal incident (travelled home Friday and found nothing to eat), alluded to briefly as evidence for the ruling; one real event with little development.
A generic illustration of an insult and retort typical of that locale, cited as evidence; speech with no specific event.
The Elders of Pumbedita teach Rav Yosef Creation in exchange for the Chariot and he then refuses; mainly teaching and speech, but with conflict and a turn.
A prayer leader performs the confession per Rabbi Meir and Rabba rebukes him; one real event followed by dialogue.
A sale case followed by Rav Ashi's ruling; nothing else is narrated to change, so under the R-C0 limit it is not a story.
Rav Yosef says he did not hear the teaching and Abaye reminds him; speech only, no conflict beyond normal discourse.
An incident only mentioned as brought to court and resolved by a ruling; no narrated action or change.
An unnamed scholar resolves to go to Eretz Yisrael, goes and questions Rabbi Abba about a reported ruling; a journey framing mainly halakhic dialogue.
Eyewitness reports of what sages wore on fast days, cited as evidence of practice; bare reports with nothing following.
Shmuel reports asking seafarers to identify a substance; an inquiry cited as information, no event.
Rabbi Yannai's student habitually refrains from challenging him on festival Shabbatot and Yannai applies a verse to him; a custom with only a verbal response, little change.
Abaye throws a clod at goats and Rabba rules he must return them; one event followed by a ruling whose outcome is not narrated.
A bare report of how Rav acquired the garden, cited as evidence for his ruling.
Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi eating caper buds and challenges him; one real event followed by halakhic dialogue.

A real incident (pledge written, ketubah lost, denial, witnesses, claim of payment) brought before R. Hiyya, but it is mostly claims and counterclaims resolved by a ruling, a courtroom case with little narrated change.
A habitual practice of Abaye's mother followed by the Gemara's objection; a custom that leads nowhere.
A lexical dispute illustrated by a one-line report of a man hawking willow; a bare report cited as evidence with no story development.
Exegetical opinions followed by a meeting with Elijah that only frames a question and answer; setting plus Q&A without conflict is not a story.
An illustrative case of two rabbis each swearing about Rav's teaching; speech acts in ordinary scholarly disagreement, cited to define a legal category.
