A local custom reported to Rav Yosef, who orders a demonstration, followed by legal debate; the outcome is only implied and nothing further is narrated.
Reish Lakish's legal argument addressed to the Elders of the South; pure speech in scholarly debate.
The narrative of Hananiah son of Azzur's false prophecy and death is a biblical episode retold; the following segment is legal discussion about it.
Shmuel veers off the road and Rav Yehuda questions him; one real action followed by a question and answer, mainly speech.
Forbidden fat falls into a pot and Rav Asi considers how to measure, then the Rabbis challenge him; one event followed by legal discussion with nothing changing.
A description of a recurring Temple practice and Rava's personal custom embedded in legal-exegetical discussion; no one-time event.
A sale, the buyer's distress and the seller's reassuring promise form a small incident, but what follows is only legal discussion of the promise's validity.
The vote in the upper story of Nitza's house only frames a halakhic ruling; no narrated event beyond the decision.
A bereavement and Rabba bar bar Hana's intentions corrected twice by colleagues; one real event, then mainly speech.
R. Akiva visits Ginzak, cannot answer questions, then goes to the study hall and learns the answers; some action and change, but mainly questions and answers.
Rav sees Rav Kahana wash his hair and rebukes him with a verse; Kahana feels cursed. One event and mainly speech, with some conflict.
A one-line report of a wonder (wheat raining on Adi the Arab) cited to show a case is possible; nothing follows.
A man sold his property and came before Rav Yeimar who ruled; coming before a rabbi and a ruling is not enough.
A man dies claiming no brothers, followed by legal debate and a ruling; one event then discussion, not even borderline.
Rav goes to a graveyard and divines the causes of death, cited as evidence of his view; some action and a discovery, but little development.
Rabbi Elazar's dream of Rabbi Yohanan is only mentioned to back an exegetical explanation. Nothing else happens and there is no change, so it is legal discussion.
A bare report of Rav Nehemya's examination practice, followed by a dispute over which law it belongs to. Nothing follows from the act.
Rabbi Abbahu recites a baraita and Rabbi Yohanan dismisses it. This is ordinary scholarly rebuke in the study hall, speech only.
Rabba dozes off and Abaye notices. The rest is a short exchange citing the mishna, so it is mainly speech with one small event.
A question put to Rav and his ruling, then a follow-up question and answer. A legal Q&A with no narrated event.
Abaye reports changing his own practice after hearing a teaching. The habit changes, but it is a first-person report of practice with little narrative.
Two incidents cited as precedent. Baitos's scroll is a bare report of practice, and the other is a scroll brought before Rabbi and ruled fit, with no further change.
Rav throws date pits into the oven and Rabbi Hiyya corrects him. One real event followed by a halakhic remark, cited as the source of a ruling.
Minyamin states his marriage plans to keep the conversion law. It is a statement of intent cited as evidence, with no narrated event.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav and a difficulty is raised. This is pure legal discussion.
A man brings his mixed wine before Rav Hisda and receives a ruling. Coming before the rabbi is the only event, and no change is narrated.
Levi checking his baraita collection is a sourcing note inside legal argument, followed by an answer for Reish Lakish.

A case arises and Rav Ilish proposes a wrong ruling. Rava rebukes him, Rav Ilish is embarrassed, and Rava comforts him with a verse. The emotional reaction and its resolution count as events and change.
An animal is brought before Rav Ashi, he rules, and Ravina challenges the ruling. A case before a rabbi followed by ordinary debate.
The table is removed, young Abaye protests, and Rabba explains. There is a real event, but it is mainly a short exchange illustrating the law.
Rabba decrees a fast and the rain fails to come, then people challenge him and he gives a long defense. These are real events with conflict, but mostly speech and no resolution.
A setting, Rabbi Zeira finding Rav Yehuda in good spirits, frames a series of questions and answers. Like Shabbat 147a, a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Rabba bar Rav Huna finds Rav Huna eating porridge with his fingers and asks why, and Rav Huna cites a teaching. A setting plus a question and answer, with nothing following.
An incident, a fetus moving after its mother's death, is alluded to only as an objection inside the legal discussion. It is barely narrated.
Rav remarks to Rabbi Hiyya and is answered with an explanation of Rabbi's practice. Speech with no event and no conflict.
Ben Zakkai's examination of witnesses about fig stems is an incident cited and alluded to as legal evidence; the rest is discussion of his identity and biography.
Rav Huna hears a man chiseling a millstone on the festival and curses him: one event plus a speech reaction with conflict, nothing follows.
A bare statement that Rav Yosef had not heard a teaching; the illness is the translator's gloss, no narrated event.
Alexa died in Lod, all Israel gathered to eulogize him, and Rabbi Tarfon prevented them: several narrated actions with a change, though cited as legal evidence.
Rabbi Abbahu's ear ailment and the instruction he received frame a medical recipe; no further action or outcome is narrated.
The Sages wished to rule a sandal fetus pure and Rabbi Yannai objected: a halakhic disagreement in speech, ordinary rabbinic discourse.
Students ask and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua answers with a list of his lifelong practices: question and answer about habits, no event.
Mostly a halakhic exchange about Ameimar's practice, but it ends with Ameimar's death, implied to be caused by Rav Ashi's remark: weak causality, mainly speech.
A heretic poses an exegetical challenge and Rava answers: speech-only debate without real conflict or event.
Rabbi Hiyya insults Rabbi Shimon's voice, he goes to his father, who supplies a retort: mainly speech with conflict and one minor action.
Baitos ben Zonin and the Sages exchange a halakhic question and answer; ordinary discourse, no event.
Shmuel tells Rav Hana to gather ten men so he can state a halakha: an instruction in speech, nothing happens.
A son steals flax sheaves and his father in response vows him out of his property, then sets a condition: incident with causality and change, followed by a legal question.
A loan with a conditional pledge of wine serves only as the occasion for legal discussion of asmakhta; no further action or change is narrated.
A halakhic dispute on the day Ravya bar Kisi died, and they made a mnemonic of it: real events with weak causality and little change.
Rav Pappa visits Mar Shmuel, sees a mezuza and asks a halakhic question: a setting plus a question, not enough for a story.
A disintegrating lung was brought before the study hall and ruled tereifa: one event followed by a ruling, nothing else changes.
A report of Shmuel's father's habitual practice of preparing ritual baths, leading nowhere.
The Sages fail to come, Rav Ashi questions Rav Kahana and learns Rava's ruling forty times: mainly a teaching exchange with minor events, like Ketubot 50a:10.
Ulla riding with two sages, an attribution dispute, his angry look and Rabba bar bar Hana's explanation: mainly speech with conflict and some action.
Scholarly exchange between Ulla and Rav Yehuda about the mishna; silence and afterthought are ordinary dialectic, no event beyond speech.
Rava's praise leads to a visit and a test of questions that leaves Rav Nahman stumped; mainly speech, but there is a visit and a change of standing.
An incident (the daughters outran the sons) is only alluded to as evidence, with minimal narration of the outcome.
A report of Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's practice of refusing wine and beer, cited for its halakhic reason; nothing follows from it.
A woman comes before Rav Yirmeya disputing a receipt; mostly speech with conflict, and the incident's resolution is not narrated.
A case brought before the Sages followed by a general ruling; no further narrated action or change.
Rabbi's recollection of eating fruit outside the sukka is a bare report cited as halakhic evidence and analyzed.
One act (taking a share) brought before Abaye and ruled on; nothing changes afterwards.
A single sale followed by an ordinary halakhic challenge and reply between Abaye and Rabba.
Transmission of three rulings and colleagues' agreement; teaching and speech without conflict or event.
Encounters that only frame a halakhic question-and-answer about a dislocated femur; setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Hypothetical legal case in a baraita with a tannaitic dispute.
An incident only named, resolved by a ruling, then ordinary sharp scholarly debate.
A halakhic question and answer between Rav Hamnuna and Rabbi Zeira; speech only.
Ameimar reports an incantation told him by the chief of witches; speech content, no event.
A ruling permitting moving a corpse, then a challenge and retort; the ruling is the only event and no change follows.
A planter's stipulation and loss serve as a case for disputed rulings; no narrated outcome beyond the legal discussion.
Rabbi Elazar's arrival only frames a halakhic question and answer about the mishna; setting plus Q&A is not a story.
A historical persecution decree prompts Rabbi Zeira to institute a deferred fast; one real event, then mostly speech and a scriptural justification.
Rav Yehuda's hand demonstration explains a term; no story.
A heretic challenges Rav Kahana and he answers; speech only, but with conflict between a heretic and a sage.
A man travels to Eretz Yisrael and asks Rabbi Abba two halakhic questions; the journey only frames a question and answer, which is not a story.
Bare report that Rav Mordekhai accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi a long distance; nothing follows.
Rabbi reads Lamentations, the book falls from his hand in distress, and he exclaims; real events and an emotional reaction, but minimal development.
Rav Sheshet's habitual practice with his explanation; a custom that leads nowhere.

A woman confesses grave sins to Rav Hisda, he tells her to prepare shrouds, and she does not die (or, in the other version, dies): an incident with an outcome. Segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary on it.
Litigants come before Rav Yitzhak bar Ami and he rules on the path width; coming before a rabbi and a ruling is not a story.
A bird fell into kutah and Rav Hinnana permitted it, with Rava's praise; one event followed by a ruling and discussion.
Rabbi Akiva asks a halakhic question in the Emmaus market; the setting only frames a question and answer.
Rabbi Yohanan's habitual reclining posture cited in legal give-and-take; a practice, not an event.
Rava intends to expound the divine name publicly and an old man objects; mainly speech with conflict and implied change.
Ulla's visit where Rav Yehuda opened sold barrels is a single act cited as evidence within legal discussion.
Ravin reports a halakha and Rabbi Yirmeya rebukes the Babylonians; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, no event.
Rav Yosef's custom on Shavuot with his explanation; a habit that leads nowhere.
Habitual practices of Rabba bar Avuh and Rabbi Hanina and a curse/explanation; reports of practice with no event following.
Rav Tahlifa ruled like Shmuel and Rav criticized it; a ruling and a rebuke cited as proof in the legal discussion, no narrated change.
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna asks several sages the same question and complains; question-and-answer with a sharp retort, ordinary Talmudic discourse.

Rav Nahman retracts the next morning, explaining he had not eaten meat the night before; mainly speech, but with a change of position and a reason rooted in an event. Segments 4-5 are halakhic discussion.
Ravina and Rav Adda are asking Rava a question when rain falls and they enter the synagogue, justifying it; real events but little change, mostly cited for the halakha.
Nehunya testified and the sages accepted his testimony; testimony and its acceptance are speech and a ruling, with no further event.
Rav Pappa's ox with a toothache breaks a lid, drinks liquor and is cured: real events and a change, but a one-line anecdote cited as evidence with little development.
One incident (the kicked safe) brought to court, then a legal discussion left unresolved; nothing further changes.
Ifera Hurmiz sends money and Rav Yosef considers its meaning; one event followed by a scholarly question and answer, with no further action.
A question sent to Rabbi Tarfon and his answer; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
A parable (mashal) illustrating Hannah's prayer, not an event that happened.
A bare report of Shmuel's purchase cited as evidence for his ruling; no response or consequence follows.
An exegetical narrative about Moses, Zipporah and the angels Af and Heima; a story about biblical characters.
Purely Gemara discussion about the Divine Voice and Gabriel's languages; no narrated event.
Habitual selling practices of Shmuel and his father evaluated by a message from Eretz Yisrael; a custom that leads to no event or change.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Adda bar Ahava and they discuss its wording; teaching dialogue without conflict.
A case (wine turned sour) followed by Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi's legal discussion; one event then discussion, nothing further happens.
First-person reports of carrying Rav Huna and Shmuel, cited as legal evidence; bare reports of acts with no continuation.
Report of a custom instituted by two sages and the Sages' ruling on it; a practice and a ruling, no narrated development.
Resh Lakish reports words he heard on a journey, used for lexical exegesis; no story.
Antoninus's habitual service of Rabbi and their exchange: a custom plus dialogue expressing devotion, with real actions but little change.
A setting (the market of Emmaus) framing an exegetical question; setting plus question is not a story.
One incident (swallowed a leech) followed by Rabbi Nehemya's ruling, then legal discussion; nothing else is narrated.
Rabbi Yosei finds food left on the stove and rules on it, cited inside a legal dilemma; a ruling, not a further event.

Wool sellers are blocked by townspeople, bring the dispute to Rav Kahana, argue, and he apportions a limited right to sell; a conflict and a ruling that changes something, but mostly a court exchange.
A one-line report that Rabbi appointed two brothers over the charity fund, cited as support; a bare report.
Only cites the Mishnah's incident by its heading and moves to a legal contradiction; no narration here.
A question answered with a rebuke, but with a physical act (throwing a clod) and conflict; mainly speech.
Exegetical narrative of Jeroboam's council and Ahijah's error, biblical figures.
Wine is brought, Ablet withdraws his hand, Shmuel responds with a ruling; real events but little change.
A case (mortgaged orchard aged) followed only by an Amoraic dispute over the law; nothing else happens.
Rav Gaza's anecdote: he made kutach and the sick asked for it; minimal events cited as evidence.
Ben Setada's entrapment and hanging is only alluded to as an instance of the procedure.
R. Hagga climbing stairs overhears a child's verses and draws an exegesis; events with little change.
Polemical dialogue between a heretic and Rav Idit; speech only, with conflict.
Report of R. Mani's purchasing practice and an elder's remark; nothing follows.
Heretic challenges R. Yishmael, a launderer intervenes and answers; speech with conflict.
Litigants' claims followed by Rava's ruling; no event beyond the dispute.
One act (dragging a bench) followed by a rebuke and a legal decree; nothing changes.
Case brought to Rav and ruled, then Rav Kahana and Rav Asi meet the owner and comment; a little more than a ruling.
Rav Yosef's act and Abaye's challenge with explanation; legal discussion of one act.
Describes Rav Yitzhak's habitual testing method; a procedure, not an event.
R. Hanina's son cut a fig tree prematurely and died; an alluded incident with causality but no narration.
An incident only alluded to as evidence: the upper victims were found dead and the lower alive.
A tanna recites before Rav and Rav disagrees; ordinary scholarly exchange.
Encounter framing a halakhic question-and-answer between scholars; standard dialogue without real conflict or change.
An exchange of insults between two gentile midwives: speech with conflict, and the killings are only alluded to in her boast.
Rava comes to the Tigris and has bar Avin rise and pray. There is a real event, but it is mainly speech and no outcome is narrated.
A lost item is brought to Rav Hisda, who rules on it. The ruling is the only thing that follows, which is R-C0's limit.
A halakha passes down a chain of whispered transmission and is then taught publicly in the market. It is teaching (speech) with a small change, followed by a dispute over the version.
Ravina comes before Rav Ashi about his wife's vow and receives a ruling. Nothing else happens.
Fasts are decreed and rain falls, then a sage responds with speech and a parable. There are events, but the passage is mainly speech and develops little.
Students discuss a point while their teacher dozes; he wakes and corrects them. This is a setting plus ordinary scholarly discourse without real conflict.
Agra brings the extra letters in his scroll before Rabbi Abba, who rules. A case and a ruling, with no other narrated action.
Rav Yehuda authorizes his son to expound and the son teaches. Teaching without conflict is speech, not a story.
An aggadic dialogue between the angels and God that explains a liturgical practice. It is speech only, with no event.
Exegesis on writing down the Oral Law, plus a report of a practice of Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish cited as evidence. The practice leads nowhere.
Ulla's eyewitness account: a bird is inspected, the Nasi summons the inspector and he leaves. These are events with weak causality, cited for their legal implication.
A dialogue about how turnips are prepared, citing the habitual practice of Rav Pappa's wife. This is a custom and a discussion, not an event.
Rabbi Zakkai teaches a baraita and Rabbi Yohanan dismisses it. This is ordinary scholarly rebuke, speech only.
Isi bar Hini arrives and Rabbi Yohanan finds him teaching. The exchange is mostly speech, but it has real conflict (the rebuke over calling Rav 'Abba the tall') and a recalled wonder.
Rav Dimi brings a fat kid and then a lean one, and both fail to show the spot, so Rabbi Yehuda teaches him orally instead. There are actions, but little change, and it ends in teaching.
Rabbi Yohanan recalls a geographic identification he made as a child, which the Elders confirmed. It is teaching and speech only.
A bare report that the Sages dissolved Rav Zutra's vow, cited to resolve a dilemma. Nothing follows.
Two short eyewitness wonders (goats sneezing at the incense, an old man smelling incense at Shiloh). These are single events with little development, the open 'I myself saw' type.
Rav Aha bar Ya'akov hears his son's blessing and they debate its wording. This is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, speech only.
A sage's statement about how he would react to suggestions; hypothetical speech, no narrated event.
A report of teachings an angel told R. Yishmael; speech/teaching with no event or conflict.
A one-time incident (bringing up the kettle, returning it, R. Hiyya's silence) cited as evidence of a view; real events but little change, so borderline rather than not.
R. Yohanan overhears a maiden praying prostrate; a real event cited as a lesson, mainly speech with little change.
Recollections of general past conditions; no particular event or change.
Rav finding a scroll is a single act cited only as the source of a teaching; nothing follows.
Rabba permits and buys the meat, his wife challenges him and he answers; real events but mainly a dialogue with mild conflict and no change.
A man takes collateral and comes before Abaye for a ruling; one event then a ruling with nothing else changing.
A man's saying and Shmuel's matching verse; speech only, no event or conflict.
A single gesture of displeasure followed by the Gemara's legal analysis; nothing narrated develops.
Exegetical teaching that Moses found three things difficult; a list of derivations, not a narrated story.
Rav's habitual announcement and a recollection of a saying; speech and custom with no event.
An exegetical narrative of Jacob and his sons at his deathbed; a story about biblical figures.
Shmuel threatens the pot merchants over prices; speech only, but with conflict.
Rabbi's instruction about his eulogies, cited as proof; speech without conflict or event.
A legal explanation invoking a directive sent during persecution; an incident only mentioned to explain a ruling, no narration.
A legal case ('one who binds another...') stated hypothetically; no event happened.
Levi and R. Shimon disagree, Levi is overruled, Psalms is brought, Rabbi's exposition leads Levi to claim leave to depart; several actions, conflict and change.
Habitual practices of sages and a recollection of a study-hall saying, within legal discussion; no event.
R. Yohanan's habitual excuse, cited as a legal proof and explained; a custom leading nowhere.
Ravina's eyewitness report: Rav Yehuda saw feces and told him to examine it. One small event plus an instruction, cited as evidence for a ruling; mainly speech.
Rav Avya is ill, misses the lecture and comes the next day; Abaye tries to placate Rav Yosef. Real events and implied tension, but the body is a halakhic question-and-answer exchange.
A man hides witnesses in a grave to trap a debtor's admission, then a ruling. A narrated incident with an action beyond coming to court, but thin and resolved only by a ruling.
Series of people coming before rabbis to have vows dissolved: a question, an answer, and the dissolution. Coming before the rabbi and his ruling is the only event.
Rav Sheshet's instruction about which direction to face, cited as evidence of his view; a practice, nothing follows.
Rebbi protested the Babylonian practice of kneading shatit, nobody listened, and he could not prohibit it. There is conflict and some events, but little change and it is reported as a note.
A wine-shop owner gave her key to a gentile woman and the study hall ruled on it. One event followed by a ruling; nothing else changes.

Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna visit the Exilarch, Rav Nahman lodges them in a sukka they consider unfit, they keep silent, he challenges them and they explain. Several actions and a conflict with a resolution.
The prayer leader recites the Pumbedita formula, the congregation tries to silence him, Mareimar intervenes, and they stop. Action, conflict and a narrated change.
Rav Yehuda demonstrating a gesture to explain a word; an exegetical illustration, not an event.
They burned R. Eliezer's purified items and ostracized him: two real events with consequence, but only a fragment of the oven of Akhnai story, cited as evidence.
Rav Kahana missed what Rav said and asked the students, who explained the ruling. Teaching and questions without conflict or change.
R. Yehuda Nesia decrees a fast, prays without rain, laments, grows distressed, and rain comes. Several events, emotion and a change.
R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei reports his father, a tanner, saying to bring hides to sit on; a practice cited as evidence, nothing follows.
An exegetical narrative of the Israelites in the wilderness growing weary and the prophets instituting Torah reading; biblical-era figures, not post-biblical sages.
Rav, Shmuel and others used to pray in the Neharde'a synagogue with a statue; a habitual practice cited as a proof in the legal argument.
A folk tale of a demon warning her son about the tree that killed his father, which then killed him, cited to explain a rule; plus Rav Kahana's habit. Events with little development, only alluded to.
R. Zeira riding while R. Hiyya bar Avin walks behind is only a setting for a question and answer about a ruling, followed by Gemara discussion; no conflict or event beyond speech.
A midrashic exchange between Ishmael and Isaac leading to God testing Abraham; an exegetical narrative about biblical characters.
King Shapur challenges Rav Hama, who falls silent, and Rav Aha bar Yaakov laments it. Mainly speech, with conflict and a failure, but no further event.
Habitual practices of Rav Huna and Rav Ashi cited as evidence; no one-time event, nothing follows.
Moses, Serah bat Asher and Joseph's coffin is a full narrative, but an exegetical retelling about biblical figures.
A disputed note and receipt brought to Rav Hama, then a ruling; nothing else is narrated.
One real act (hiding witnesses to entrap) and an exchange, followed by Rav Kahana's ruling; mainly speech with a case-and-ruling shape.
Plague spares Rav's neighborhood, people attribute it to Rav, a dream reveals the true cause: events with a revelation and change.
Hillel sees a floating skull and addresses it: one real event, then a saying.
Report of Rav Yosef's agricultural practice and its result, cited as evidence; no narrative development.
An incident only briefly alluded to as evidence (a man completed 365 naziriteships and died).
A setting (Sages entering the Yavne vineyard) framing a series of homilies; teaching is speech and there is no conflict or event beyond the setting.
Rabbi Yona's habitual secret prayer brings rain and he conceals it from his household; a habit that leads to change.
A setting at a river crossing plus a halakhic question and answer; not enough for a story.
The marten-and-pit story is only alluded to by name; the narrative must be supplied from commentary.
Sages observed a bird mauling prey, cited as evidence for a ruling; a bare observation.
Borrowed cat killed by mice (or dying from overeating) is a vivid event, but followed only by a legal dilemma and a dictum; the pail case is event-then-ruling and not a story.
The Nasi's death and an instruction about rending garments; the outcome is only implied.
Rabbi Bena'a dreamed, went to 24 interpreters, and all interpretations came true: multiple events and an outcome.
A childhood memory of a public announcement, cited as evidence for Shmuel's practice; no development.
Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir a question and he answers; a question and answer with no event or conflict.
Report of an elder's habitual practice, cited as evidence; nothing follows.
Rav visits Rav Shapir and is served a fish prepared three ways; a setting cited for a point about food, with no development.
A one-time incident (they forgot the scalpel and carried it over roofs on Shabbat) cited as legal evidence; real events but little development or change.
First-person incident: Rabbi Abbahu ate asafoetida and sat in water to avoid harm; two events and a minimal change, a minimal story cited as proof of a dictum.
A person comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi and receives a ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
A halakhic question put to Ameimar and his answer; no narrated event.
Eyewitness report of what Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi did with fruit, cited as evidence for three halakhot; no one responds and nothing follows.
A man consults Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, is praised, returns and is instructed; mainly dialogue but with movement and implied change in the man's conduct.
A reported permission followed by ordinary scholarly challenge and resolution; Rabbi Asi's astonishment is part of routine debate.
Rav Huna asks which tradition to follow and Rav Yosef answers, turning his face away; ordinary scholarly exchange without a narrated event or change.
Reports of how Abaye and Rava bowed, with a brief correction; practice cited as evidence, no conflict or change.
An army opened barrels and Rabbi Elazar permitted the wine, followed by analysis of his reason; one event then a ruling, nothing further changes.
Exegetical narrative about Micah's idol, the angels and the concubine of Gibeah; biblical characters, not rabbis.
Within a halakhic question, an incident is cited of a ewe whose punctured windpipe was sealed with a reed and lived; two events and change but only alluded to as evidence, like the Chullin 57b hen.
Rabba bar Rav Huna's declaration in a dispute with the Exilarch's house; speech only, but with genuine conflict.
Two rabbis buy goods at a pagan fair and rebuke each other; real events plus conflict, but mainly a speech exchange followed by legal explanation.
A precocious child is asked halakhic questions and answers them; question and answer without a narrated event.
Shmuel's father and Levi habitually prayed in a synagogue with a statue, cited as evidence; a custom that leads nowhere.
A man promised land to one buyer then sold it to another for more, followed by a ruling and dispute; two actions like the cow case, but the narrative ends at the legal discussion.
Rav Ashi sold a forest to a fire temple and answered Ravina's challenge; one act and ordinary halakhic exchange, nothing changes.
Rahava asks Rav Yosef, who permits, Abaye objects, and Rav Yosef reverses and sends him away; mainly speech but with a change of ruling and outcome.
A lost piece of meat brought before Rav Nahman and a ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
A legal objection and response between R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish, his silence, and later analysis; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event beyond speech.
A one-line eyewitness report of seeing the frontplate in Rome, cited as evidence; nothing follows.
Rav Hisda recounts absorbing blows from Avimi over a halakha: an alluded incident with conflict, but it is mainly a report of a teaching exchange.
Halakhic question with practices of Rav Yehuda, Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak and Rav Huna cited as evidence; bare reports of practice with nothing following.
A Sage frequenting the leather market explains a word, followed by legal discussion; no narrated event.
A girl found holding froth among barrels and Rava's ruling; one event followed by a ruling with no further change.
Rav Huna bans song and prices collapse; Rav Hisda belittles the ban and prices rise: multiple actions with causal change.

A man shows the Exilarch's wheat to thugs who seize it, the case comes before Rav Nahman who imposes liability, and the scene continues with the sages' exchange; incident with more than one action plus a ruling, like the cow case.
A needle found in a liver and a halakhic exchange about it; one event then a ruling, nothing changes.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel instructs his attendant and Rava corrects him on the law; an instruction and a ruling with no further event.
A passing allusion to a giant snake in Shapur's time raised as a legal objection; no narrative.
Rav Kahana passes a locust near his mouth and Rav tells him to remove it, cited within legal argument; one act and an instruction, no stated change.
Two reports of sages waving a willow without a blessing, cited as evidence of their view; bare reports of practice.
A dialogue of praise and comparison between Rabbi and R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei; speech only without real conflict or event.
Rav Hisda finds Rav Hananel writing from memory and states the prohibition, then legal discussion; one event and a ruling with no narrated change.
A habitual wonder said of Yonatan ben Uzziel (birds burned when he studied); a characterization with no one-time event or development.
A host asks a halakhic question, the sage refers it to Rava who answers; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
